title: A premium faith app that doesn't default to dark mode
subtitle: Redesigning Bibel TV's streaming apps to hold the German market against a global competitor
team: Design-led, with cross-functional partners. Hamburg / Berlin

sections.headline: A premium faith app that doesn't default to dark mode
sections.subtext: Bibel TV's streaming app had the deeper archive and the cultural fit, but looked a few years behind its own 2025 broadcast rebrand. The redesign had to make what Bibel TV already had feel as premium as it actually was.

sections.quote: Premium streaming means dark mode: that is the industry default. Our users want light. The question was not which trend to follow, but how to make a light interface feel genuinely premium.
sections.context: The strategic design bet at the centre of the project

sections.headline: The gap
sections.content:
Bibel TV is a broadcaster in the middle of a linear-to-streaming transformation, with apps across iOS, Android, web, and connected TV, and a broadcast archive going back generations. The app did not show it. The patterns were dated, it had not followed the 2025 broadcast rebrand, content was hard to discover, and nothing in it was built for retention.

The redesign had to close that gap: turn German-market knowledge, cultural fit, and the archive into something a user could feel in the first thirty seconds, instead of an app that looked older than the brand actually was.

sections.headline: The light-mode bet
sections.content:
The redesign gave the app a new visual language, aligned with the 2025 broadcast rebrand: lighter, warmer, and properly premium. Streaming-native patterns for discovery, search, and watch-next. Three core areas, the Mediathek, Bible reading, and reading plans.

The real bet was light mode as the primary direction, against the streaming-industry default of dark. Bibel TV's users associate darkness with something impersonal; warmth is the brand. Making a light interface feel premium is genuinely unsolved, which is why it could not stay a surface decision, it needed real colour and contrast work underneath, and a design system that could keep four platforms in step. Those became their own projects (see the related case studies), built in parallel so the redesign would be dynamic, not static.

sections.headline: Research, and a lesson about platforms
sections.content:
The work ran about nine months in three phases: competitive analysis against the global streaming apps, prototyping, then validation with staff and with users.

One lesson is worth keeping. I built the first prototype for web because web is fast, then rebuilt it on Android, because Android is the largest part of our userbase. A stakeholder had raised a specific worry on the way in: old Android screens in our userbase render gradients badly. Testing it showed the worry was real and the diagnosis was not. The banding tracks old displays, not Android. So the fix generalised past the original concern, and we now build multi-step gradients even for monochrome ones, which is what actually addresses banding. Prototype where your users are, and be willing to find that the thing everyone named was not the variable.

metrics.label: User validation
metrics.value: Bibel TV users showed a strong, research-confirmed preference for light mode, plus follow-up conversations on the redesign's premium feel (exact sample size being reconfirmed — see verification log 2026-08-25)

metrics.label: Brand alignment
metrics.after: A shared visual language across app and broadcast

metrics.label: Readiness
metrics.value: Design direction finalised and validated; moving into development with working prototype code

sections.headline: What I took from it
sections.content:
Owning the design of this app end to end meant owning what sat under it. A light-mode redesign that looks premium is not a Figma decision, it depends on the colour engine and the token system that keep it consistent and correct. Designing the surface and leaving the infrastructure to chance would have produced a demo, not a product.

And the platform lesson stuck: web-first prototyping is fast, but target-platform-first is honest.

Curious how "old Android phones render gradients badly" turned out to be about the displays and not the platform, and how that fix ended up running in every gradient the app ships now, even the plain-looking ones? Get in touch.

executive.summary: Led the redesign of Bibel TV's streaming apps into a premium, warm, light-mode experience closing the gap between the app and the 2025 broadcast rebrand. Research confirmed a strong user preference for light mode; design direction finalised and validated, moving into development.

blog.summary: A global competitor was launching a premium dark-mode faith app in Germany. Bibel TV chose light mode, because its users want warmth, not Hollywood. Here is how that bet was made.
blog.angle: Choosing against the industry default, on purpose
